[c11] Lasso Regression and Regularization: Lasso is a regression analysis method introduced by Robert Tibshirani that enhances prediction accuracy and interpretability through variable selection and shrinkage. It relies on sparse coefficients and requires careful tuning of the regularization parameter to balance model performance against excessive coefficient reduction. The method is closely related to elastic net and linear support vector machines, serving as a specialized approach for handling high-dimensional data.
[c02] Regularized Regression Techniques for Multicollinearity: This cluster focuses on regularized regression methods, particularly ridge regression and Principal Component Regression (PCR), which address multicollinearity and numerical instability in linear models. Introduced by Hoerl and Kennard, ridge regression serves as a shrinkage estimator that improves upon least square estimators by reducing variance in the presence of correlated predictors. PCR offers an alternative approach by using principal components as regressors, functioning as both a reduced rank regression and a regularized procedure to ensure efficient prediction.
[c13] Linear Regression Estimation and Regularization: This cluster focuses on linear regression methodologies, contrasting classical approaches like ordinary least squares with regularized methods such as the ridge estimator to address issues like multicollinearity. It explores theoretical guarantees through oracle inequalities and restricted eigenvalue conditions, which are crucial for analyzing sparse linear predictors. Additionally, the group distinguishes between general linear models, which handle vector responses, and multivariable models, while noting alternative estimation techniques like fixed effects.
[c05] Gradient Descent Optimization Methods: Gradient descent is a first-order iterative algorithm used for unconstrained mathematical optimization by minimizing differentiable multivariate functions. Its performance relies heavily on the properties of the objective function, such as strong convexity and Lipschitz smoothness, which determine the convergence rate. While basic implementations may suffer from slow convergence due to curvature issues, techniques like preconditioning and momentum methods can significantly improve efficiency.
[c01] Regularization Techniques for Model Generalization: Regularization is a critical method in machine learning designed to prevent overfitting and underfitting by encouraging models to learn broader patterns rather than memorizing training data. Techniques such as L1 and L2 regularization, dropout, and early stopping are employed to improve model generalization and ensure accurate predictions on unseen data. From a Bayesian perspective, these methods often correspond to imposing prior distributions on model parameters, effectively balancing the data likelihood with complexity constraints.

## Community reports
[c09] Random Forests and Ensemble Variants: Introduced by Leo Breiman, random forests are an ensemble learning method that utilizes bootstrap samples and randomized node optimization. Variants such as extremely randomized trees modify the training process by using the whole learning sample and random cut-points for splitting. The framework has theoretical connections to kernel methods and adaptive nearest neighbors, while specialized versions like Enriched Random Forest address high-dimensional data challenges. Additionally, model compression techniques can transform these complex ensembles into interpretable born-again decision trees.
[c07] Decision Tree Models and Variants: This cluster focuses on decision trees as interpretable white box models that utilize Boolean logic for classification tasks. It details various algorithms like ID3, CART, and Fuzzy Decision Trees, along with metrics such as information gain and Gini impurity used for splitting nodes. The community also contrasts these transparent structures with black box models like artificial neural networks and explores advanced variations like decision graphs that improve predictive accuracy.
[c04] Bias-Variance Trade-off in Machine Learning: The bias-variance decomposition analyzes a model's generalization error by breaking it down into bias, variance, and irreducible error components. High bias leads to underfitting by missing relevant feature relations, while high variance causes overfitting by modeling random noise in the training data. Various methods, such as dimensionality reduction and adjusting hidden units, are employed to manage this trade-off and optimize model performance. Additionally, computational constraints often necessitate accepting controlled bias to significantly reduce variance and overall estimation error.
[c01] Regularization Techniques for Model Generalization: Regularization is a critical method in machine learning designed to prevent overfitting and underfitting by encouraging models to learn broader patterns rather than memorizing training data. Techniques such as L1 and L2 regularization, dropout, and early stopping are employed to improve model generalization and ensure accurate predictions on unseen data. From a Bayesian perspective, these methods often correspond to imposing prior distributions on model parameters, effectively balancing the data likelihood with complexity constraints.
[c06] Regression Methodologies and Collinearity Challenges: This cluster examines various regression techniques, including hierarchical linear models and group lasso, alongside critical issues regarding variable selection and collinearity. It highlights how methods like stepwise regression can misuse variance inflation factors, leading to invalid statistical inferences such as biased standard errors and p-values. Additionally, the report details how perfect collinearity arises from redundant variables or improper dummy coding, necessitating careful model specification.

Mechanisms such as pruning are necessary to avoid this problem (with the exception of some algorithms such as the Conditional Inference approach, that does not require pruning).

[p021] In machine learning, a key challenge is enabling models to accurately predict outcomes on unseen data, not just on familiar training data. Regularization is crucial for addressing overfitting—where a model memorizes training data details but cannot generalize to new data. The goal of regularization is to encourage models to learn the broader patterns within the data rather than memorizing it. Techniques like early stopping, L1 and L2 regularization, and dropout are designed to prevent overfitting and underfitting, thereby enhancing the model's ability to adapt to and perform well with new data, thus improving model generalization.

[p129] Random forests or random decision forests is an ensemble learning method for classification, regression and other tasks that works by creating a multitude of decision trees during training. For classification tasks, the output of the random forest is the class selected by most trees. For regression tasks, the output is the average of the predictions of the trees. Random forests correct for decision trees' habit of overfitting to their training set.

[p138] For example, following the path that a decision tree takes to make its decision is quite trivial, but following the paths of tens or hundreds of trees is much harder. To achieve both performance and interpretability, some model compression techniques allow transforming a random forest into a minimal "born-again" decision tree that faithfully reproduces the same decision function. Another limitation of random forests is that if features are linearly correlated with the target, random forest may not enhance the accuracy of the base learner. Likewise in problems with multiple categorical variables.

[p120] A decision tree is a simple representation for classifying examples. For this section, assume that all of the input features have finite discrete domains, and there is a single target feature called the "classification". Each element of the domain of the classification is called a class. A decision tree or a classification tree is a tree in which each internal (non-leaf) node is labeled with an input feature. The arcs coming from a node labeled with an input feature are labeled with each of the possible values of the target feature or the arc leads to a subordinate decision node on a different input feature.

[p126] Requires little data preparation. Other techniques often require data normalization. Since trees can handle qualitative predictors, there is no need to create dummy variables. Uses a white box or open-box model. If a given situation is observable in a model the explanation for the condition is easily explained by Boolean logic. By contrast, in a black box model, the explanation for the results is typically difficult to understand, for example with an artificial neural network.

[p032] In the process of regression model selection, the mean squared error of the random regression function can be split into random noise, approximation bias, and variance in the estimate of the regression function. The bias–variance tradeoff is often used to overcome overfit models. With a large set of explanatory variables that actually have no relation to the dependent variable being predicted, some variables will in general be falsely found to be statistically significant and the researcher may thus retain them in the model, thereby overfitting the model.

[p034] In this process of overfitting, the performance on the training examples still increases while the performance on unseen data becomes worse. Thus, early stopping has been suggested as a solution. As a simple example, consider a database of retail purchases that includes the item bought, the purchaser, and the date and time of purchase. It's easy to construct a model that will fit the training set perfectly by using the date and time of purchase to predict the other attributes, but this model will not generalize at all to new data because those past times will never occur again.

[p030] As an extreme example, if the number of parameters is the same as or greater than the number of observations, then a model can perfectly predict the training data simply by memorizing the data in its entirety. (For an illustration, see Figure 2.) Such a model will typically fail severely when making predictions. Overfitting is related to both the complexity of the chosen model and how well it is optimized during training.

[p128] In a decision tree, all paths from the root node to the leaf node proceed by way of conjunction, or AND. In a decision graph, it is possible to use disjunctions (ORs) to join two more paths together using minimum message length (MML). Decision graphs have been further extended to allow for previously unstated new attributes to be learnt dynamically and used at different places within the graph. The more general coding scheme results in better predictive accuracy and log-loss probabilistic scoring. In general, decision graphs infer models with fewer leaves than decision trees.

The lasso method assumes that the coefficients of the linear model are sparse, meaning that few of them are non-zero. It was originally introduced in geophysics, and later by Robert Tibshirani, who coined the term.

[p006] Lasso was introduced in order to improve the prediction accuracy and interpretability of regression models. It selects a reduced set of the known covariates for use in a model. Lasso was developed independently in geophysics literature in 1986, based on prior work that used the  [formula] penalty for both fitting and penalization of the coefficients.
